REP: Victor, thanks for meeting with me. I know store managers don't get many quiet hours, so I'll be efficient. How are clinical services going at this store?
CUSTOMER: Vaccines are strong. We're one of the top stores in the district for flu shots. Last season we did almost two thousand, which is a lot for a store our size.
REP: What other programs has corporate added this year?
CUSTOMER: Medication therapy reviews in the spring, then adherence calls in the summer. Each one comes with a target and a dashboard. The dashboards go to the regional director every Friday, so the store managers feel it.
REP: How are your pharmacists feeling about all that?
CUSTOMER: Tired. Honestly, the last thing I want is to walk into the Monday huddle and announce another program. My pharmacists are already doing vaccines, reviews and three hundred scripts a day. Adding testing is going to burn them out.
REP: I appreciate you being straight with me, and burnout is a real risk. I'd rather not add something that makes Mondays worse. Which part of the day is hardest for your pharmacists right now?
CUSTOMER: Late afternoon. Four to seven. Everyone picks up on the way home from work, and that's also when sick people show up. That's when we get the most complaints about wait times, too. Our survey scores are lowest in that window.
REP: That's helpful, because it changes how I'd set this up. Most of the chain stores we work with don't put testing on the pharmacist during the rush at all. The technician does the swab and runs the reader, and the pharmacist reviews the result on the screen, which takes about a minute. The stores that do best cap testing at two slots an hour from four to seven, so it never stacks up. A lot of managers tell us it actually takes pressure off, because their pharmacists stop having the same ten-minute conversation about where the nearest urgent care is. Would a tech-led setup with capped slots ease that worry for you?
CUSTOMER: Tech-led makes a difference. If it's on my techs, with a cap, I could see it working.
REP: Good. What does corporate look at when they decide whether a store gets a new service?
CUSTOMER: Volume and staffing. They'll want to see that we have enough sick traffic and enough tech hours. They also look at what the neighboring stores are doing, so they don't put two services in the same area.
REP: Do you have a sense of how much sick traffic you see in a week?
CUSTOMER: We sell a lot of cold and flu product. During flu season, probably thirty people a week ask us where they can get tested. My techs keep a sticky note with the urgent care's number on the register because they get asked so often.
REP: Thirty a week is strong. At thirty-five dollars a test, even a third of those would add about three hundred and fifty dollars a week in service revenue, plus the prescriptions you'd keep. That's the kind of number corporate responds to, and it's easy to track, because the reader logs every test and exports a weekly report you can forward as it is.
CUSTOMER: Compliance will be the issue. They'll want to know who's responsible for the waiver and for the documentation if something goes wrong.
REP: The CLIA certificate is held at the store level, with your pharmacist-in-charge as the director of record, and our compliance packet includes the documentation templates and the referral protocol that most chains have already approved. I can send you the packet another regional chain used. Would that help your compliance team?
CUSTOMER: It would. They like seeing that someone else already approved it. Anything that saves them from writing a policy from scratch moves faster.
REP: Then here's what I'd suggest. I'll send you the compliance packet and a one-page summary for your district manager today, and I'd like to set up a thirty-minute call with you and her next week. Does Thursday the 1st at ten work on your end?
CUSTOMER: Let me check. Thursday the 1st at ten, yes, I'm on the schedule. I'll forward the invite to her.
REP: Great. I'll send the invite with the packet attached, so she has it before the call.
CUSTOMER: Sounds good, Daniel.
